title: KRYN: A local coding agent and the benchmark that grades it
story_key: story|title:kryn a local coding agent and the benchmark that grades it
content_excerpt: A coding agent that runs entirely on a Mac with a 9B model, the preregistered benchmark I built to test it against plain OpenCode, and what it found: no uplift yet, a 60% token cut that made the agent worse, and an agent that kept changing its own tests. The best coding agents in the world run in someone else's data center. They're fast, they're good, and every file you show them leaves your machine and costs money per token. I wanted the other version: an agent that lives on my laptop, costs nothing to run, keeps the code where it is, and is good enough to do real engineering work. Not autocomplete. Something you'd hand a bug to. KRYN is that project. It's a coding workspace for Apple Silicon that puts OpenCode 's agent loop in front of a local Qwen3.5-9B model and wraps the whole stack in the parts a shared laptop needs: a verified installer with rollback, a memory guard, a session record that survives restarts, and recovery when something stops. v1.0.0 shipped on 2 October 2026 and v1.0.1 on 23 November. The long-term target is frontier-adjacent coding: close enough to the hosted agents that the difference stops mattering for most tasks. KRYN doesn't claim that yet, and the reason this write-up is long is that I built the machinery to know when it can. Half of this project is the product. The other half is a benchmark rig strict enough that I'll believe it when it says yes. The roadmap turns the distance into eight gates. A local coding agent has three constraints a hosted one doesn't, and a fourth that every agent has. Memory is shared. The target machine is an M4 Max with 48 GiB of unified memory, and it's also my normal working laptop with a browser and everything else open. The model, its key-value cache, the agent, a test runner and a headless browser all compete for the same pool. If the agent pushes the machine into swap, the laptop becomes unusable, and nobody keeps a tool that does that. The model is small. A 9B model at 6-bit quantization is about 8 GB of weights. It can write code, call tools and follow a plan, but it makes more mistakes than a frontier model, recovers from them less gracefully, and loses the thread sooner. Context is expensive. Every token of context costs memory and prefill time on local hardware. Long sessions compact, and compaction summaries can be wrong. Agents grade their own homework. The model says it's done. Whether it is done is a separate question, and on a small model the gap is wide. The first frozen task I ran

title: Show HN: An agent skill that optimizes code with falsifiable hypotheses
story_key: story|title:an agent skill that optimizes code with falsifiable hypotheses
content_excerpt: Agents that optimize your code like an algorithm engineer: a falsifiable hypothesis before every experiment, correctness checked after every change, one reviewable patch per accepted change, and a PDF report of the whole session. A skill for Claude Code and Codex, from the Algorithm Engineering Group at Heidelberg University. Algorithm Engineering is a cycle of design, analysis, implementation and experiment, driven by falsifiable hypotheses. AAE hands this cycle to an autonomous agent. During setup you agree with the agent on the benchmark, the metric, the correctness assertions and the budget; then it runs on its own. A falsifiable hypothesis: "changing X will improve the metric by roughly Z, because ..." Predict direction and size of the effect before measuring, from profiling and analysis. Run the benchmark; keep the change only if it is better and still correct, otherwise revert. From the report of the KaHIP kaffpa session: 122 experiments, 69 hypotheses, 41 patches, 3.9x faster in total. In Codex, install the skill with scripts/install_codex_skill.py and call it with $aae ; any other agent can follow AAE.md . To try it first, run the 10-minute quick-start example : a slow but correct shortest-path program with a benchmark and a correctness check. Sessions share what they learned: the knowledge base collects optimization techniques and experiment results, and agents read it before they start. Contributions from your own sessions are welcome. David A. Bader, Adil Chhabra, Ernestine Großmann, Monika Henzinger, Alexander Noe, and Christian Schulz. Agentic Algorithm Engineering: Improving Shared-Memory Exact Minimum Cuts. In 13th DIMACS Implementation Challenge Workshop: Network Flows 2.0, OASIcs, 2027. To appear. Preprint: arXiv:2609.07204 .

title: Sandboxing AI Coding Agents: Nono vs. Docker Sbx vs. Microsandbox vs. OpenShell
story_key: story|title:sandboxing ai coding agents nono vs docker sbx vs microsandbox vs openshell
content_excerpt: In this blog post, we compare four major sandboxing tools for AI coding agents in a hands-on approach: nono, Docker Sandboxes, Microsandbox and OpenShell. We describe what makes a good sandbox and our evaluation criteria. We provide a comparison table at the end that hopefully helps you decide which tool is right for you. Disclaimer: we are not affiliated with any of the tools discussed in this article. According to JetBrains' Developer Ecosystem Survey 2026 , 90% of professional developers used AI coding agents at work at least weekly between May and July, and 68% used them daily. Meanwhile, Stack Overflow's 2026 survey found that only 7% of respondents trust AI output for important work decisions. What this shows is that AI coding agents are widely used, but at the same time, few of their users trust them for important decisions. Not only shouldn't they be trusted for important decisions because they can hallucinate or take unwanted actions by mistake, but they also have inherent vulnerabilities that attackers can exploit to manipulate their behavior and force them to take malicious actions. Indeed, prompt injection is still an unsolved problem. The 2025 CaMeL paper describes a defense mechanism to solve it but it's impractical to implement in practice. Meanwhile, Anthropic reports that prompt injection attack success rate (ASR) against Fable 5, Opus 5 and Sonnet 5 is as low as 0.0% and therefore made Auto mode the default mechanism to automatically classify commands to be executed in Claude Code in August. Even though Anthropic claims a 0.0% ASR, Johann Rehberger showed that he obtained a 60-80% ASR by asking the agent to summarize a website that contained a novel trick not in Anthropic's static benchmark. One should read AI labs ASR numbers with a pinch of salt and Claude Code's Auto Mode is not a replacement for running the agent in a sandbox. The sandbox is a strong protection for when the agent gets manipulated. Prompt injection shouldn't be underestimated. There are many different input vectors malicious instructions can be delivered from and they may not always be visible to you. Here are some examples. The idea here is that if the agent runs in a sandbox, even if it's manipulated by malicious instructions, there's only so much it can do. The sandbox limits the blast radius. And this is why sandboxing tools are all the rage lately. This also applies to agents that take unwanted actions by mistake or due to a hallucination, regardless of whether th

title: Skip the DRAM Tier: MoRI UMBP Runs the Agentic KV Cache on NVMe
summary: On AMD Instinct™ MI355X GPUs, a MoRI UMBP KV pool on NVMe matched a DRAM pool of the same size within 1% for Kimi-K3 on vLLM, and drives that hold a day of agent KV cost less than DRAM that holds 31 minutes.
story_key: story|title:skip the dram tier mori umbp runs the agentic kv cache on nvme
content_excerpt: Most of the traffic in agentic serving is multi-turn sessions that resend long prefixes. In the AgentX benchmark replaying real Claude Code sessions, the median turn is 142K input tokens, and over 96% of those tokens are a prefix the server has already seen [3] . A KV cache hit means the prefill node only has to process the small delta. A miss forces a full recomputation of the prefix, which burns GPU time and delays the first token. In our 42 runs of Kimi-K3 on vLLM, raising the KV cache hit rate by 1% of prompt tokens, for example from 95% to 96%, was worth about 10% more throughput (Figure 3). A KV cache hit needs the session’s prefix to still be in memory when its next turn arrives. With dozens of sessions open at once, memory runs out. GPU memory goes first, and host DRAM is the usual next tier. But DRAM fills too: Kimi-K3 wrote 2.3 to 4.6 TB of KV to the pool an hour in our runs, so a 1.8 TB DRAM pool, which lists at about $76,000, holds only the last 23 to 47 minutes of it. That led us to a simple question: why not skip the DRAM tier and put vLLM’s KV pool straight on NVMe? We tried it on AMD Instinct™ MI355X GPUs with UMBP, the KV cache pool in AMD’s open-source MoRI library. At the same size, NVMe matched DRAM’s throughput within 1% on Kimi-K3, in two sets of runs on different machines (Figure 1). On a second workload with longer prompts, NVMe came within 1% of a DRAM pool of the same size. The NVMe pool has no DRAM tier: DRAM only buffers new KV on its way to the drives and stages reads, about 80 GB against the DRAM pool’s 1.8 TB. And NVMe’s cost follows the KV it writes, not the KV it holds, so drives rated for Kimi-K3’s writes cost less than that DRAM pool and hold a full day of KV. “Agentic workloads keep sessions open for minutes or hours, and their KV cache quickly outgrows GPU memory and host DRAM. Results like these, with NVMe keeping up with DRAM at the same pool size, change how we think about sizing KV cache capacity in AI clusters. We’re glad to see this work done in the open, in vLLM and MoRI.” — Dennis Kennetz, Principal Infrastructure Engineer, Oracle Cloud Infrastructure DeepSeek already keeps agent KV caches on SSD: the deployment notes for its DeepInfer engine describe three days of retention for agent traffic, on about 14.4 TB of SSD per GPU [4] . This work references DeepInfer for the idea of keeping the KV cache on SSD and for two of its techniques, layer-wise loading and bounded replay, which we test on vLLM below. Figure 1.
llm_summary_1line: On AMD Instinct™ MI355X GPUs, a MoRI UMBP KV pool on NVMe matched a DRAM pool of the same size within 1% for Kimi-K3 on vLLM, and drives that hold a day of agent KV cost less than DRAM that holds 31 minutes.
summary_1line: Describes MoRI's UMBP KV cache pool on AMD MI355X GPUs, which placed vLLM's KV cache directly on NVMe without a DRAM tier and matched DRAM pool throughput within 1% for Kimi-K3 at the same pool size.

title: How to build and maintain an agentic evaluation
story_key: story|title:how to build and maintain an agentic evaluation
content_excerpt: AI evaluations help shape which systems people build, adopt, and trust. An evaluation gives a system tasks, checks its answers or actions, and produces a score. Building and maintaining a useful evaluation therefore takes real work: defining tasks that reflect domain expertise, scoring them reliably, and checking that the results support the claims made. When methods, code, and data stay private, that work is harder for others to scrutinize or build on. Open source offers a means to build stronger, more frequently updated, and more comparable evaluations and the infrastructure around them. Existing tasks, environments, and tools give builders a starting point, so their effort can go to domain expertise and validation. Sharing how an evaluation was built, including what went wrong, lets others find errors, improve it, and reuse it. The Hugging Face hub is the home for AI evaluation: we host around 3500 eval leaderboards and have seen about a 16X growth in eval datasets on the hub in the past year , to about 17000 datasets. In recent months, we have also incorporated support for agentic abstractions that are relevant to evaluation. For example, Traces that store an agent’s work in an easily reviewable and sharable way; Benchmarks that highlight datasets used to evaluate models with leaderboards; and Environments that show datasets used as agentic RL or evaluation environments. In the research community, AI evaluation terminology is notoriously inconsistent . The glossary at the end defines each term we use and notes the other names you may come across. AI evaluation design has evolved in three forms as language models have become more capable and able to perform more complex work: question answer, agentic, and teams or swarms. Question-answer benchmarks such as MMLU (2020) and GPQA (2023) measure knowledge and reasoning through the answers models produce. As models became capable of planning and using tools, agentic benchmarks such as SWE-bench and WebArena expanded the scope to resolving software issues and completing tasks on websites. These tasks require evaluation setups that account for the environment in which the system operates and the changes it makes. Lately, research on multi-agent systems has started to add another dimension: how agents coordinate and what they accomplish together. This includes decentralized swarms , teams managed by an orchestrator , and specialized agents collaborating on scientific work . Figure 1 shows a rough timeline of th

title: Who Grades the Agent? Privilege Separation for Coding-Agent Benchmarks
summary:
Benchmarks for AI-based coding agents are a staple of the current AI landscape, because they are the leading way to measure the performance of LLMs. Their scores guide business and research decisions. Evaluating coding agents is challenging, since they are able to manipulate their evaluation infrastructure to artificially achieve better scores. Grading an agent's solution often requires running its code, which can then manipulate the evaluation process. BenchJack, an automated benchmark auditor, recently reached near-perfect scores on nine of ten popular agent benchmarks without actually solving their tasks. Agents already do this unprompted, as OpenAI's July 2026 Hugging Face incident showed.
  Building on secure systems design, we introduce SplitBench, a privilege separation framework for evaluating coding agents and the first in the scientific literature to separate running a task's tests from judging their results. Even an agent whose code takes over the entire test environment cannot forge a pass, because a trusted grader holds the expected answers. We show that real-world benchmarks (e.g., Terminal-Bench, DeepSWE) can be ported to the SplitBench framework with minimal effort and high fidelity: 180 of 202 tasks convert, and SplitBench agrees with the native graders on 98.7% of agent attempts. We attack the converted tasks in the worst case, where adversarial agents can read all the grading code but not the expected answers. SplitBench blocked 75% of their attempts; the rest mostly reveal weaknesses in the original tasks' tests rather than flaws in SplitBench.

title: Decision Columns as an Index: Interpretable Embeddings for Explainable Entity Matching and Search
summary:
Business data systems must determine whether records refer to the same entity and retrieve records satisfying requests whose decisive properties are implicit. As agents act on these records, both tasks require auditable reasons. Dense embeddings perform well but offer opaque coordinates, cannot be filtered by meaning, and require corpus re-encoding to add new properties. We propose interpretable embeddings built from decision columns: each column stores a decision model's calibrated answer to a natural-language question, with outcomes yes, no, or not stated. A record's embedding is its answers across an ordered set of questions. Similarity decomposes exactly into per-question contributions, and new questions add coordinates without altering existing ones.
  On public product benchmarks, question-space retrieval matches dense candidate generation statistically in a retrieve-then-verify entity matcher, while providing exact explanations for accepted matches. Questions derived from retrieval failures triple mean reciprocal rank without re-encoding prior answers. For search, inferring the attributes of a suitable result outperforms encoding only the literal request, and combining question-space and dense scores improves retrieval, though not at our prespecified confidence threshold. A single small neural network predicts the full interpretable vector from an existing dense embedding, enabling corpus backfilling from a few thousand labeled rows at roughly 1/200 the cost. We position interpretable embeddings as a complementary, readable retrieval channel for explaining matches, filtering on attributes, and extending indexes as failures expose missing facts.

title: Inkling 2 Mini on vLLM: Day-0 Support for a Looped Model
summary: vLLM supports Thinking Machines' Inkling 2 Mini from day 0: a looped MoE that runs its middle layers three times, with per-pass KV caches, gated messages between passes, fused kernels and DSpark speculative decoding.
story_key: model:vllm|variant:mini|title:inkling 2 mini on vllm day 0 support for a looped model
content_excerpt: Thinking Machines announced Inkling 2 Mini today. vLLM supports it and its variable-loop research checkpoint, TML-d24-varloop-research , on day 0 on NVIDIA Blackwell, Hopper and DGX Spark. Inkling 2 Mini is a looped model: its middle 12 layers run three times per token with shared weights, each pass with its own KV cache and gated messages from the pass before. It is a multimodal MoE with 26B total and 3.5B active parameters, up to 1M tokens of context and a native DSpark speculator. We provide a Docker image with Inkling 2 Mini support, vllm/vllm-openai:inkling-2-mini . You can serve the model with: And the variable-loop research checkpoint, here with 2 passes and one KV cache shared across passes: Figure 1. The prelude and coda run once; the loop core runs three passes, each reading messages from the one before. Prelude, core, coda. The 24 layers split into a prelude (layers 0–5), a loop core (layers 6–17) and a coda (layers 18–23). The prelude and coda run once each; the core runs three passes with shared weights, and the coda continues from the last pass. Each group of six layers is one block of the block attention residuals used in Inkling 2 Small, so one pass of the core produces exactly two blocks. Every pass starts from the prelude's output. A plain looped model feeds pass p's output into pass p + 1. Here, all three passes start from that same output, and pass p + 1 sees pass p only through messages. Messages are read at every sublayer. From the second pass on, each core sublayer input (the attention's query, key and value inputs and the MLP input) gets its own message, read from the previous pass's two blocks by an attention-residual read with a learned query per layer and input type. A rank-64 controller then merges the message into the input, per channel: With 12 core layers and 4 inputs each, every later pass reads 48 messages per token. Because the query, key and value inputs get different messages, the sliding-window layers, which project all three from one input in the first pass, take three separate inputs in later passes. Each pass keeps its own memory. Every core layer has a KV cache and a conv-state cache per pass, so pass p attends to the keys and values that pass p computed for earlier tokens. The model has 24 layers but 48 KV caches and 48 conv-state caches. DSpark draft from inside the loop. The 3-layer DSpark draft reads the target's hidden states at four layer visits: one in the prelude, one each in the second and third passes, and

title: claude-code v2.1.327
summary:
What's changed

  • Added a confirmation before /install-github-app changes a repository
  • Added claude mcp add-json <name> - to read the server's JSON from stdin, so tokens can stay off the command line; not available inside a Claude Code session
  • Added a line when a resumed session's earlier messages can't be loaded
  • Added a list in /status of broken agent, skill, command and output style files, keybinding errors, an unavailable sandbox, ignored permission settings and hook matchers that never match
  • Added a note in /config when other settings override a row
  • Added x-claude-code-managed-settings-checksum to the gateway hint headers; sent where managed settings set CLAUDE_CODE_GATEWAY_HINT_HEADERS=1, including where they already do
  • Added support for naming a session's billing group with the attributionProject setting, for Claude apps gateways that set admin.billing_group_tag
  • Added /tui classic as the name for the non-fullscreen renderer; /tui default still works
  • Remote Control: Fixed stopping the server in worktree mode deleting a running session's git-ignored files, such as .env
  • Fixed self-hosted runners with --use-anthropic-git-proxy deleting a non-empty directory named by GIT_CONFIG_GLOBAL at startup: the runner now keeps it, ignores the variable and warns
  • Fixed claude mcp add and claude mcp remove with project scope deleting other top-level keys from .mcp.json, such as $schema or another tool's servers
  • Fixed /export overwriting an existing file without asking: the dialog now asks, and /export <name> keeps the file and says to run /export
  • Fixed a command you had allowed still running after you pressed Stop, when the approval arrived after a restart, in cloud and self-hosted runner sessions with no feature flags loaded
  • Fixed Enter closing /teleport's load error screen
  • Fixed a click followed by Enter in /plugin installing or disabling a plugin
  • Fixed a half-typed ! command running on an extra Enter after the usage limit menu
  • Fixed some --disallowedTools rules with parentheses in their content
  • Fixed auto mode ignoring some wildcard PowerShell allow rules that name a script with .\, such as PowerShell(.\scripts\build.ps1 *)
  • Fixed a running Code Mode script in auto mode getting permission prompts and denials once Claude started a second script that auto mode also allowed
  • Changed some pre-started background sessions to be discarded after an account change
  • Changed a workflow paused at a usage limit in the terminal to stay paused after a login, until the earlier login returns or you type a prompt
  • Fixed a nested claude with its own token being refused by forceLoginOrgUUID: commands that don't get the session's token no longer get its CLAUDE_CODE_OAUTH_SCOPES; set it on any that need it
  • Fixed headless sessions losing stored messages on resume when a message was sent again with the same UUID after the process was killed
  • Fixed cases where a session resumed after an empty reply or a killed command lost an answer, or brought back a rewound prompt, after another crash or a move to the background
  • Fixed a remote session forgetting messages sent after Stop was pressed during a restart, if Claude Code then crashed
  • Fixed tasks created after /clear being lost, and cleared tasks coming back, when a cloud or self-hosted runner session with no feature flags loaded resumed later
  • Fixed a compaction right after a reply cut at the output token limit losing that reply's tool call and its result
  • Fixed a settings change from /config and similar commands failing to save with no warning; a line under the prompt now says so
  • Fixed /rewind closing without a word when some files could not be restored
  • Fixed pasted images being dropped when the prompt starts with a file path such as /tmp/a.txt
  • Fixed agents passed with --agents being lost once plugins loaded or reloaded
  • Fixed a plugin's agent being dropped when resuming a session from the --resume picker
  • Fixed Claude Code refusing to start when https_proxy or HTTPS_PROXY is a bare host:port and neither its input nor its output is a terminal (the desktop app, an SDK, cron)
  • Fixed Claude Code on Linux sometimes returning to the shell while restarting itself at startup, such as after the first sign-in to a Claude apps gateway or when turning on Code Mode
  • Fixed claude -p hanging before its first request when the fetch of a model's settings stalled, such as at a proxy; it now goes on without them after 10 seconds
  • Fixed the screen staying blank or frozen after a brief out-of-memory error
  • Fixed a rare display fault that could freeze the screen or end the session
  • Fixed cloud sessions breaking when a program left thousands of connections open to the session's network proxy
  • Fixed a turn hanging when a mod's $.model.complete or $.model.classify call met a usage limit: the call now gets the API's error at once; mods should handle that error
  • Fixed stalls on a compaction reply with thousands of unclosed tags and on some very long WebFetch URLs; WebFetch now refuses a URL over 2,000 characters before any permission prompt
  • Fixed a message with thousands of @ mentions stalling before Claude replies; only the first 100 mentions are now looked up as files
  • Fixed the prompt freezing after rejecting a write to a very large file; a rejected write now shows a short preview
  • Fixed a crash when a burst of keys reached the search box in /plugin
  • Fixed a false crash report and exit code when a suspended session resumes, or at exit, where a Linux security policy blocks a process from signalling itself
  • Fixed remote MCP servers staying disconnected after a longer outage such as a VPN drop: most servers on other machines reached by hostname over https are now retried in the background for about a day
  • Fixed Edit refusing with "File has not been read yet" after a compaction on unchanged files outside the project that Claude had already read in full
  • Fixed Grep repeating or skipping results when paging with head_limit and offset; content and count results are now sorted by file path

  • Fixed a Stop hook that failed to run being shown as having reported a problem
  • Fixed focus view keeping a finished reply hidden while a Stop hook was running
  • Fixed Claude getting a long managed PostToolUse hook output twice when a mod added context to the tool call
  • Fixed /model listing the wrong models in some terminal sessions when a project's .claude/settings.json sets ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL to an LLM gateway

  • Fixed the selected session leaving the screen in claude --resume and /resume when branch names or folder paths are long

  • Fixed an MCP server's long question being cut off after one row, text fields hiding long pastes with no sign, and a doubled divider line in /plugin's options and /login's Bedrock and Vertex steps

  • Fixed Ctrl+C twice not closing /chrome from its browser list

  • Fixed exit not saying that a worktree was kept
  • Fixed /hooks help naming input fields that do not exist
  • Fixed question dialogs naming ctrl+g after the external editor key was rebound
  • Fixed two sign-in error messages that pointed to the Claude subscription option on computers where forceLoginMethod is set to console
  • Fixed /config saying the dialog was dismissed instead of "Set theme to …" after changing the theme
  • Bug fixes and reliability improvements
  • Improved the speed of a session's first Bash command: shell start-up files may now run before it's approved, even if it's refused; set CLAUDE_CODE_DISABLE_SHELL_HEAD_START=1 to turn this off
  • Improved commits on newer models and in PowerShell: Claude is now told not to commit files that likely contain secrets

  • Improved resuming very long sessions: a transcript read that ends early is now retried once, so messages are lost less often
  • Improved subagent answers that hit the output token limit twice: they now more often come back whole or say up front that they are partial
  • Improved long replies on unrecognized models: a reply cut at 32,000 output tokens now continues with a limit of 128,000
  • Improved the reminder about a completed subagent after compaction: if Claude can't read the agent's output file, it is now told to ask the agent with SendMessage
  • Improved the warning shown when an API key and an Anthropic profile are both set: it now says which one is in use and how to switch to the profile

  • Improved startup time on Windows when PATH points to Git for Windows' bin folder, by starting git.exe directly instead of through its launcher
  • Windows: Improved PowerShell tool speed by up to about half a second per command
  • Improved how soon the Bash tool's diff of changed files is ready in auto and bypass permissions modes
  • Improved speed of the Bash permission check on very deeply nested missing paths on macOS and Linux, and of secret masking on very long text with a URL
  • Improved transcript search to find text in edits and written files
  • Improved speed of reading large PNG images, and the quality of the JPEG sent in their place

  • Improved narrow terminals: /status, forms and detail screens lay out better, /model and /effort fit at about 40 columns, and key hints such as ←/→ to adjust stay
  • Improved /install-github-app: the repository, secret and API key steps use the standard list and keys, with shorter messages, a spinner and clearer errors
  • Improved /desktop: the download question is a standard list instead of y/n

  • Changed auto mode's notice about falling back to billed classifier requests to say that an upcoming release removes the fallback; each action it would have checked will be asked about or denied
  • Changed auto mode to ignore more allow rules that run any package, like Bash(pnpm dlx *), and path or version forms of ones it already ignored (/usr/bin/npm run:*); the safety check decides those
  • Changed /sandbox and most /config value lists to be unnumbered outside screen reader mode; use the arrow keys and Enter
  • Changed Bash commands whose variables expand to very long text to be denied, with a message that says to use shorter values or a file
  • Changed the PowerShell tool to ask before one more command, even under a rule naming it; if nothing answers, it's refused unless a whole-tool rule, auto mode or bypass permissions mode allows it
  • Changed a subagent resumed by a sibling's message to follow the session's permission settings; it may now ask, or be refused where nobody can answer
  • Changed --worktree with a relative --add-dir beside the launch folder to give the Bash sandbox that folder, not one beside the worktree
  • Changed some --worktree starts with a relative --add-dir above the launch folder, such as .., to give the Bash sandbox, and a --bg session, only the worktree
  • Changed Claude in Chrome to refuse uploading some credential files; attach those to the page yourself
  • Changed artifact approval in organizations that require it for each new artifact: an artifact that only a plugin created or allowed can be refused
  • Changed sessions with nobody to ask to refuse a new artifact at once, with no permission prompt, in organizations that require approval of each one
  • Changed the Artifact tool to refuse calls once settings turn Artifacts off, in sessions already running too
  • Changed the Artifact publish prompt to stop offering "don't ask again" in subagents and after a background task result, someone else's message or a compaction
  • Changed claude plugin eval to keep its deny rules over a plugin's permission hook, and to flag calls the hook let through
  • Changed MCP server logs to record the mode, action, and field names of elicitation requests and hook answers, not their full contents
  • Changed most prompts to ignore answers other than Esc for a moment after resuming with fg
  • Changed Code Mode to no longer refuse to start when an installed mod hooks tool calls; an administrator can still keep Code Mode off in managed settings
  • Changed subagents launched without a model to stay on the model they started on when resumed, including after /model
  • Changed the first subagent on a model to wait up to 1.5 seconds (10 in claude -p) for that model's settings from Anthropic, instead of starting without them
  • Changed restarted background subagents, and turns that start by themselves, to wait for plugins to load

  • Changed subagent progress summaries in terminal sessions on Amazon Bedrock, Google Vertex AI and Microsoft Foundry to be written from short notes, not the whole conversation, using far fewer tokens
  • Changed non-interactive (-p) mode to run fewer git commands before the first request
  • Changed first-run setup to skip terminal setup in remote VS Code, Cursor and Devin Desktop sessions, where it cannot change settings

  • [VSCode] Improved speed when Claude makes several edits in a row: queued edits share one wait for new problems; a problem may be reported with a later edit
  • [VSCode] Improved @-mention file search speed in large workspaces when rg is on your PATH; results now rank much as in the terminal, with less tolerance for typos
  • [VSCode] Improved startup: the model picker is ready at once in folders opened for the first time, empty windows and worktrees, except on third-party providers
  • [VSCode] Changed a chat edit's diff to stay open and keep asking for approval when a terminal session in the same window sends a prompt
  • [VSCode] Removed unused tools from the IDE connection (openFile, saveDocument, getOpenEditors and related)

title: Topology Hub Optimal Transport: Eliminating Long Context Dilution at Flash Speed
summary: Long-context models use sparse or structured attention to avoid quadratic cost, yet retrieving a small set of relevant facts embedded among hundreds of thousands of distractors degrades as normalization mass disperses with length. Hub-and-spoke optimal transport (OT) replaces the dense $L \times L$ matrix with a linear-size graph over local windows and $K$ shared hubs balanced by Sinkhorn scaling. Building on block-wise tail refinement and fixed-support transport topology (arXiv:2605.08123, arXiv:2609.07954), we introduce Topology Hub Optimal Transport (THOT): (1) bounded-support capacity gating via simplex sparsemax ($O(L\log L)$) or sorting-free token-local thresholded ReLU ($O(L)$), driving excess distractor mass to zero; (2) a three-sweep $1+2$ annealed row-closed Sinkhorn schedule that damps bipartite residuals; (3) an exact rank-$(D+2R+1)$ One-Reference-Tile adjoint in batched split-factor Triton kernels (BF16 Tensor Cores, FP32 potentials); and (4) a chunked exclusive-prefix causal variant with verified zero future leakage. On NVIDIA L4, sparsemax THOT trained at $L=128$ reaches 97.40% zero-shot recall of fixed bindings at $L=262{,}144$ under pure task loss ($α=0$) and 98.83% at $α=0.05$ (matched by $O(L)$ thresholded ReLU at $α=0.05$, vs. 80.60% at $α=0$), while softmax-gated hub OT drops to 3.52%. In bidirectional operator microbenchmarks, our kernel runs forward+VJP in 100.1 ms at $H=8, D=64, L=262\mathrm{K}$ (2.2x faster with 4.0x smaller compiler temporaries than latent softmax) and 1.34 ms vs. 4.37 ms for cuDNN FlashAttention at $L=4{,}096$; multi-layer LM runs use the unfused path. Zero-shot WikiText-103 multi-needle retrieval hits 100.00% (128/128 queries at $L=65\mathrm{K}$) vs. 0.78% for short-trained RoPE FlashAttention, and compact 4-layer WikiText-4K runs show modest causal and masked LM gains.

title: DPMA: Learning to Compress Mixture-of-Experts Models
summary: Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) architectures offer high computational efficiency, but storing all experts requires substantial memory and limits deployment on resource-constrained hardware. Most retraining-free MoE compression methods commit to either pruning or merging experts, often with a uniform compression ratio across layers. We introduce DPMA (Differentiable Prune Merge Absorb), which jointly learns compression operations and layer-wise expert allocation through gradient descent under a global expert budget. Separate learnable coefficients allow DPMA to prune experts, merge their parameters, and absorb their routing contributions by forwarding routing weights to retained experts. These coefficients and expert assignments are optimised to match the original model's outputs on calibration data while its weights remain frozen. Across four MoE models, eight multiple-choice benchmarks, and five compression ratios, DPMA achieves the highest accuracy averaged over benchmarks and compression ratios on each model among the evaluated methods. At $75\%$ expert reduction, it outperforms the strongest baseline on every model, with gains of up to $6.7$ percentage points.

title: Release 2.75.0 corresponding to NGC container 26.11
summary:
Triton Inference Server

The Triton Inference Server provides a cloud inferencing solution optimized for both CPUs and GPUs. The server provides an inference service via an HTTP or GRPC endpoint, allowing remote clients to request inferencing for any model being managed by the server. For edge deployments, Triton Server is also available as a shared library with an API that allows the full functionality of the server to be included directly in an application.

New Features and Improvements

  • PyTorch backend: Added AOTI BF16 input/output support.
  • THIRD-PARTY-NOTICES.txt is now included in the containers.
  • Fixed a use-after-free in the dynamic batcher and a preserve_ordering completion-slot issue on response-cache hits.
  • Prevented silent gRPC stream cancellations under backpressure.
  • Bounded the decompressed HTTP inference response size in the client library.
  • Perf Analyzer: Honored supplied output shapes, propagated the binary exit code, tagged the wheel as platform-specific, and limited profile-data export to the needed inputs and outputs.
  • Python backend: Now logs when the backend stub exits on a crash signal.

Known Issues

  • The Triton TensorRT-LLM Backend container image is not included in this release.
  • vLLM's v0 API and Ray are affected by vulnerabilities. Users should consider their own architecture and mitigation steps which may include but should not be limited to:
    • Do not expose Ray executors and vLLM hosts to a network where any untrusted connections might reach the host.
    • Ensure that only the other vLLM hosts are able to connect to the TCP port used for the XPUB socket. Note that the port used is random.
  • When using Valgrind or other leak detection tools on AGX-Thor or DGX-Spark systems, you might see memory leaks attributed to NvRmGpuLibOpen.
  • Valgrind or other memory leak detection tools may occasionally report leaks related to DCGM. These reports are intermittent and often disappear on retry.
  • CuPy has issues with the CUDA 13 Device API in multithreaded contexts. Avoid using tritonclient cuda_shared_memory APIs in multithreaded environments until fixed by CuPy.
  • TensorRT calibration cache may require size adjustment in some cases, which was observed for the IGX platform.
  • The core Python binding may incur an additional D2H and H2D copy if the backend and frontend both specify device memory to be used for response tensors.
  • A segmentation fault related to DCGM and NSCQ may be encountered during server shutdown on NVSwitch systems. A possible workaround for this issue is to disable the collection of GPU metrics tritonserver --allow-gpu-metrics false ....
  • When using TensorRT models, if auto-complete configuration is disabled and is_non_linear_format_io:true for reformat-free tensors is not provided in the model configuration, the model may not load successfully.
  • When using Python models in decoupled mode, users need to ensure that the ResponseSender goes out of scope or is properly cleaned up before unloading the model to guarantee that the unloading process executes correctly.
  • Triton Inference Server with vLLM backend currently does not support running vLLM models with tensor parallelism sizes greater than 1 and the default "distributed_executor_backend" setting when using explicit model control mode. In attempt to load a vllm model (tp > 1) in explicit mode, users could potentially see failure at initialize step: could not acquire lock for <_io.BufferedWriter name='<stdout>'> at interpreter shutdown, possibly due to daemon threads. For the default model control mode, after server shutdown, vllm related sub-processes are not killed. Related vllm issue: vllm-project/vllm#6766. Please specify "distributed_executor_backend":"ray" in the model.json when deploying vllm models with tensor parallelism > 1.
  • When loading models with file override, multiple model configuration files are not supported. Users must provide the model configuration by setting parameter "config" : "<JSON>" instead of custom configuration file in the following format: "file:configs/<model-config-name>.pbtxt" : "<base64-encoded-file-content>".
  • TensorRT-LLM backend provides limited support of Triton extensions and features.
  • The TensorRT-LLM backend may core dump on server shutdown. This impacts server teardown only and will not impact inferencing.
  • The Java CAPI is known to have intermittent segfaults.
  • Some systems which implement malloc() may not release memory back to the operating system right away causing a false memory leak. This can be mitigated by using a different malloc implementation. Tcmalloc and jemalloc are installed in the Triton container and can be used by specifying the library in LD_PRELOAD. NVIDIA recommends experimenting with both tcmalloc and jemalloc to determine which one works better for your use case.
  • Auto-complete may cause an increase in server start time. To avoid a start time increase, users can provide the full model configuration and launch the server with --disable-auto-complete-config.
  • Auto-complete does not support PyTorch models due to lack of metadata in the model. It can only verify that the number of inputs and the input names matches what is specified in the model configuration. There is no model metadata about the number of outputs and datatypes. Related PyTorch bug: pytorch/pytorch#38273
  • Triton Client PIP wheels for ARM SBSA are not available from PyPI and pip will install an incorrect Jetson version of Triton Client library for Arm SBSA. The correct client wheel file can be pulled directly from the Arm SBSA SDK image and manually installed.
  • Traced models in PyTorch seem to create overflows when int8 tensor values are transformed to int32 on the GPU. Refer to pytorch/pytorch#66930 for more information.
  • Triton cannot retrieve GPU metrics with MIG-enabled GPU devices.
  • Triton metrics might not work if the host machine is running a separate DCGM agent on bare-metal or in a container.

Client Libraries and Examples

The client libraries and examples are available in this release exclusively via the Ubuntu 24.04–based NGC Container. The SDK container includes the client libraries and examples, Performance Analyzer, and Model Analyzer. See Getting the Client Libraries for more information.

ManyLinux Assets (early access)

This release was compiled with AlmaLinux 8.9 based out of manylinux_2_34 and can be used on RHEL 9 and later versions.
See the included README.md for complete details about installation, verification, and support.
This release supports ensembles. Confirm CUDA, TensorRT, ONNX Runtime, PyTorch, and Python versions in the shipped README.md.
Some optional backend features such as the PyTorch backend's TorchTRT extension are not currently supported.
